newsitem.title: UK: S&P rates Kazakstan BB minus foreign currency.
newsitem.headline: S&P rates Kazakstan BB minus foreign currency.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Tuesday it assigned its BB-minus long-term and B short-term foreign currency ratings to the Republic of Kazakstan.
In addition, S&P said it assigned its BB plus long-term and B short-term local currency ratings to the republic's tenge-denominated debt.
"The outlook on the long-term ratings is stable," S&P said.
S&P said Kazakstan's ratings are supported by:

-- The country's relatively successful shift to a marked-based economy which, combined with a sharp tightening of fiscal and monetary policies, has led to a stabilization of output this year and a steep reduction in inflation, officially projected at 27.5 percent at year-end 1996 (compared to 1256 percent and 60 percent at year-end 1994 and 1995, respectively).

-- A low general government debt burden of around 20 percent of GDP this year, and light net public external debt equivalent to about 18 percent of exports that compare favorably with those of other rated sovereigns in the double-B' category. With about 22 percent of exports, Kazakstan's total external debt service (including short-term debt and trade credit) is also less than that of most sovereigns with BB category foreign currency ratings.

-- The country's improving external liquidity position, with reserves now covering 3-4 months of imports. Given the country's export and foreign investment potential due to its oil and mineral resources, Kazakstan's external position should remain manageable, despite an expected temporary widening of the current account deficit to about 5 percent of GDP in 1997/1998 as imports recover from their depressed levels. Kazakstan's creditworthiness, however, is constraint by:
-- The country's untested political system, and short track record of orthodox macro-economic policies and debt management.
-- Continued weakness in the government's revenue performance, with the brunt of fiscal consolidation still borne by an unsustainable compression of spending.
-- The risk of slippages in enterprise and banking sector reforms, which could undermine investor confidence and jeopardize monetary and fiscal control.
-- The challenge of boosting private sector savings and deepening financial intermediation with the real sector.
-- The need to secure trade and transit arrangements with its neighbors, particularly Russia, to take full advantage of its oil and mineral wealth.

The higher tenge credit rating reflects the government's taxation powers and control of the domestic financial system. Very low outstanding tenge-denominated debt, in the country's nascent domestic capital markets, as well as the government's commitment to continued tight fiscal and monetary policies also support the local currency ratings.

The growing commitment of the country's leadership to systemic reforms and prudent economic management should improve the conduct of fiscal policy and keep public and external debt burdens at manageable levels over the medium term. At the same time, increased exploitation of the country's oil and mineral reserves is expected to foster sustained economic growth and attract higher levels of external capital inflows, Standard & Poor's said.
